analysis.one_liner: Bans a list of toxic chemicals, including PFAS and BPA, from food packaging.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced June 9, 2026 with five Democratic cosponsors, sits in the Senate health committee with no action since referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal food safety law to declare an entire list of chemicals unsafe for use in food packaging — including PFAS ('forever chemicals'), phthalates, BPA and related bisphenols, formaldehyde, styrene, asbestos, and benzene. Once a chemical is on the list, packaging containing it could no longer be legally sold for food contact after a two-year phase-in. It also requires regulators to consider effects on infants, children, pregnant women, and workers when reviewing substitute chemicals, and leaves stricter state laws and consumers' right to sue in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially infants, children, pregnant women, and the elderly, who would eat less of these chemicals leaching from packaging into food; workers in packaging plants and communities near chemical facilities, who get explicit protection in the bill; and manufacturers already selling PFAS-free packaging, who gain a level playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deems 15 classes of substances unsafe as food contact substances, including ortho-phthalates, PFAS, BPA/BPS/BPF, formaldehyde, styrene polymers, asbestos, benzene, and ethylene oxide, making packaging that contains them illegal after a two-year phase-in. [S2]

When companies petition to use a replacement chemical, the FDA must consider potential adverse effects on vulnerable populations, defined to include infants, children, adolescents, pregnant women, the elderly, workers, and communities with disproportionate exposure. [S2]
The bill is written as a floor, not a ceiling: it says nothing in it preempts stricter state or local laws, or any consumer's right to sue under state tort or consumer protection law. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Chemical makers that produce PFAS, phthalates, bisphenols, and styrene, and food packaging manufacturers that use them, would bear reformulation and compliance costs, some of which would likely be passed to food companies and shoppers as modestly higher packaging costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill bans chemical classes outright rather than by safety testing, so some substances on the list might be used in forms or amounts that pose little risk, forcing reformulation costs without a demonstrated health benefit in every case. [S2]

Food packaging is used everywhere at once, so a two-year transition could raise short-run packaging costs for restaurants, grocers, and packaged-food makers, which tend to flow to consumers in prices. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health rationale is substantial: PFAS, phthalates, and bisphenols are among the most studied food-contact chemicals of concern, and reducing exposure touches nearly everyone who eats packaged or take-out food. The main honest cost is transition: packaging supply chains would have to reformulate on a two-year clock, and prices could tick up slightly. The bill softens this by allowing industry petitions to approve safe substitutes and by keeping state laws and lawsuits intact.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has received no further action so far.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on June 9, 2026, joined by Senators Merkley, Markey, Duckworth, and Wyden, all Democrats. [S2]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction. [S4]
Five cosponsors, all Democrats, are listed on the bill. [S3]
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached; if the bill sits, PFAS and other food-contact chemical makers keep the status quo and food packaging manufacturers avoid reformulation costs.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Ed Markey, Tammy Duckworth, Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill its only recorded support.

sides.party_line_note: All five cosponsors are Democrats and no Republican support or recorded opposition appears in the record; the bill's fate so far has simply been inaction in committee rather than a fight.

industries.note: The bill makes PFAS, phthalates, bisphenols, styrene polymers, and several solvents illegal in food packaging, cutting off a major product market. Consumers currently ingest trace amounts of these chemicals through packaging contact, so the industry's revenue stream runs against the public's exposure reduction.

Makers that use the listed chemicals must reformulate within two years, a real compliance cost; manufacturers already producing PFAS-free and phthalate-free packaging gain a level playing field. Shoppers' food-safety gain comes at the price of some transition costs likely passed into prices.

These firms would need compliant packaging within two years and could face modest cost increases, but many chains have already moved away from PFAS coatings after state bans and consumer pressure. They bear adjustment costs rather than an existential threat.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term bill referred to the Senate HELP Committee with five Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support rarely reaches a markup, let alone the floor; unless a bipartisan cosponsor signs on or the committee leadership schedules it, the likely path is that it sits until the Congress ends in January 2027.
